ConfigSetItem.description:
One configuration assignment from the admin panel.

``value`` is deliberately untyped: the settings model decides what is
acceptable, and ``core.config_edit.check_value`` refuses the rest against
that model rather than against a second, drifting schema here. It is
bounded, though -- see :data:`CONFIG_VALUE_MAX_CHARS`.
ConfigSetItem.title: ConfigSetItem

SessionReopen.description:
Optional display overrides for a history "reopen".

The ``argv`` and the backend come from the *record* (see
``routes.sessions.reopen_session``): the endpoint replays what was
recorded, and the caller does not get to dictate what is spawned. These
fields only rename the replay or move its working directory.
SessionReopen.title: SessionReopen

TotpConfirm.description: The code that turns a *pending* TOTP enrolment into an active one.
TotpConfirm.title: TotpConfirm

get.description: Effective configuration, labelled by whether a reload can apply it.

put.description:
Write configuration values to the config file, then apply what can be.

The write goes through :mod:`wsctl.core.config_edit` -- the same code the
CLI's ``config set`` uses -- so both entry points keep the author's inline
comments, type-check the value, validate the whole file and roll back
rather than publish a document the server cannot start from.

Only fields that a reload can actually reach are writable. A ``restart``
field is refused with that reason rather than accepted and silently doing
nothing until someone remembers to restart.

get.description:
The cast for one session -- while it runs *and* after it is gone.

A session that had ended made ``owned_session`` 404 and the only other
door (``GET /api/recordings``) is admin-only, so a plain user could never
get their own recording back. The row outlives the session; so should the
download.

post.description:
Recreate a session the way ``sid`` originally ran.

The ``argv`` comes from the *record*, not from the request body. The
endpoint name promises "the way it originally ran"; taking the caller's
word for it made ``sid`` decorative -- any id, including one that never
existed or belonged to someone else, answered 201 -- while letting the
client dictate what would be spawned. History's "reopen" is a replay of
what was recorded, and only of that.

get.description:
Liveness **and** identity.

The pid is not decoration: during a rolling restart two instances share
the port for a moment, and a plain 200 on this endpoint cannot tell the
orchestrator which one answered. Without it the gate passed as soon as the
*predecessor* replied, the predecessor was retired, and the successor was
not yet serving -- a refused-connection window, which is the entire thing a
rolling restart exists to avoid.

schema.title: Response Healthz Healthz Get

get.description: Readiness: every dependency a request may need must be usable now.
